title: SEX DURING MENSTRUATION: The Biblical Command Most Christians Never Discuss
paragraphs:
SEX DURING MENSTRUATION: The Biblical Command Most Christians Never Discuss
There is a verse sitting quietly in Leviticus that almost nobody talks about in church—and once you actually read what God said, the question becomes impossible to ignore.
There are Bible verses Christians quote constantly.
John 3:16.
Philippians 4:13.
Psalm 23.
Jeremiah 29:11.
And then there are verses we seem to walk past very quickly.
Verses that make the room uncomfortable.
Verses that touch the bedroom.
Verses that force husbands and wives to ask whether surrender to God includes places in their marriage they assumed belonged entirely to them.
This is one of those passages.
And before going any further, something needs to be made unmistakably clear.
Menstruation is not shameful.
A menstruating woman is not disgusting, spiritually inferior, morally guilty, or somehow farther from God.
The Bible never teaches that menstruation itself is a sin.
Yet the same Bible does contain a remarkably direct command concerning sexual intercourse during menstruation.
And whatever conclusion a Christian eventually reaches about how that command relates to believers under the New Covenant, intellectual honesty requires us first to hear what the text actually says.
Because sometimes the most dangerous way to handle Scripture is not openly rejecting it.
Sometimes it is simply never talking about it.
Leviticus 18:19 reads in Hebrew:
וְאֶל־אִשָּׁה בְּנִדַּת טֻמְאָתָהּ לֹא תִקְרַב לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ
Ve’el-ishshah beniddat tum’atah lo tiqrav legalot ‘ervatah.
A close rendering is:
“And you shall not approach a woman in the menstrual condition of her impurity to uncover her nakedness.”
Those words deserve more than a nervous glance.
The Hebrew נִדָּה — niddah carries the idea of menstrual separation or the condition associated with menstruation.
לֹא תִקְרַב — lo tiqrav means “you shall not approach” or “come near.”
And לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ — legalot ‘ervatah, literally “to uncover her nakedness,” belongs to the sexual language of Leviticus 18.
In other words, this is not merely a vague ancient statement about hygiene.
The immediate context is sexual conduct.
Leviticus 18 speaks about forbidden sexual relationships, and verse 19 places intercourse during menstruation inside that discussion.
Then Scripture becomes even more explicit.

Leviticus 20:18 describes a man lying sexually with a menstruating woman and says that he has exposed “the source of her flow” while she has exposed “the source of her blood.” Under Israel’s covenant administration, the text attaches the severe sanction of both being “cut off” from their people.
That is uncomfortable.
But discomfort does not give us permission to pretend the passage does not exist.
Yet here is where careful Bible reading matters enormously.
Leviticus also contains an extensive system of ritual impurity, and ritual impurity is not identical to moral wickedness.
This distinction changes everything.

Leviticus 15 discusses menstruation alongside bodily discharges. The same chapter says that a man becomes ritually unclean after an emission of semen. Ordinary marital intercourse also made both husband and wife ritually unclean until evening.
So “unclean” cannot automatically mean “sinful.”
A bodily condition could make someone ceremonially unclean without making that person morally guilty.
That means a woman experiencing her monthly period was not committing a sin merely because she was menstruating.

She was experiencing a normal bodily process within a covenantal system where blood, bodily emissions, life, death, holiness, sanctuary access, cleansing, and separation carried profound symbolic meaning.
This is where careless preaching can deeply wound women.
God was not declaring women filthy.
Menstruation was not female guilt.
And no Christian husband should weaponize Leviticus to humiliate his wife, treat her body with disgust, or make her feel spiritually contaminated.
Jesus Christ never gives men permission to turn holiness into cruelty.
But another mistake lies on the opposite side.
Recognizing the ceremonial dimensions of Leviticus does not allow us simply to erase Leviticus 18:19.
Why?
Because the prohibition does not appear only in the ritual-purity regulations of Leviticus 15.
It appears in Leviticus 18 among sexual prohibitions.
It appears again with a penalty in Leviticus 20.
And generations later, Ezekiel uses strikingly similar language.
When Ezekiel 18 describes a righteous man, among the behaviors mentioned is that he does not defile his neighbor’s wife and does not approach a woman during her menstrual impurity.
Ezekiel 22:10 likewise includes violating women during menstrual impurity among Jerusalem’s covenant offenses.
So anyone claiming that the Bible treats the subject as completely insignificant has to wrestle honestly with more than one passage.
But Christians must wrestle with something else too.
The cross.
Jesus Christ fulfilled the Law.
The New Testament radically changes the believer’s relationship to the ceremonial structures of the Mosaic covenant.
We do not bring Levitical animal sacrifices to an altar.
We do not maintain Israel’s sanctuary purity system.
We do not assume that every regulation given to covenant Israel transfers unchanged into the church.
Christ has inaugurated the New Covenant, and Hebrews repeatedly points us toward the fulfillment found in Him.
This is why Christians must resist two opposite temptations.
One says:
“It is in Leviticus, therefore every detail applies to Christians exactly as it applied to ancient Israel.”
That is too simplistic.
The other says:
“It is in Leviticus, therefore Christians can ignore it.”
That is also too simplistic.
The real question is harder:

What does this command reveal about God’s holiness, sexuality, blood, covenant order, self-control, and the way His people should honor Him with their bodies—and to what extent does the specific prohibition continue as Christian moral obligation?
Faithful Christians have not all answered that final question identically.
The New Testament never gives Christians a sentence directly repeating, “Do not have intercourse during menstruation.”
That fact matters.
We should not manufacture a New Testament command that is not explicitly there.
At the same time, the Old Testament passages remain Scripture, and their repeated treatment of the practice means Christians should not mock, conceal, or casually dismiss the subject either.
Romans 15:4 reminds believers that what was written beforehand was written for our instruction.
Second Timothy 3:16 says that all Scripture is God-breathed and profitable.
So perhaps the mature Christian response is not:
“How quickly can I explain this verse away?”
Perhaps it is:
“Lord, what are You teaching me here—and am I willing to obey You even when obedience reaches somewhere private?”
That question goes far beyond menstruation.
Because suddenly the bedroom becomes a mirror.
We live in a culture trained to believe that desire creates entitlement.
I want it.
Therefore I should have it.
I feel it.
Therefore it must be right.
We even carry that thinking into marriage.
But biblical marriage never means unlimited sexual entitlement.
First Corinthians 7 teaches profound mutuality between husband and wife, but the same passage assumes love, agreement, and consideration—not coercion.
Christian sexuality is never merely about what someone can obtain from another person's body.
It is supposed to become another place where Christ is Lord.
That changes how a husband looks at his wife when she is bleeding, hurting, exhausted, cramping, uncomfortable, or simply does not want sexual intercourse.
She is not an instrument for his appetite.
She is someone made in the image of God.
Someone he vowed to love.
Someone for whom Christ died.
And perhaps there is something deeply countercultural about a husband being capable of saying:
“My desire does not rule me.”
“I can wait.”
“I can hold you without demanding something from you.”
“I can love you when your body cannot give me what I want.”
“You are more valuable to me than sexual gratification.”
That kind of restraint does not weaken intimacy.
It can reveal love.
And wives need the same heart of surrender before Christ.
Marriage is not two people asking how close they can get to the boundary without technically crossing it.
Christian marriage is two redeemed sinners learning to ask:
“How can our bodies glorify Jesus?”
There is a deeper issue hiding underneath this entire conversation.
Who owns the locked rooms of your life?
We happily give Jesus Sunday morning.
We give Him worship songs.
We give Him Bible verses posted on Facebook.
We give Him Christian captions.
But what happens when Christ walks toward the bedroom door?
What happens when Scripture touches money?
Pornography?
Secret fantasies?
Resentment?
Sexual boundaries?
Forgiveness?
Pride?
The habits nobody at church knows about?
Suddenly theology becomes personal.
Because Jesus did not die merely to become a decoration hanging over your life.
He died and rose again as Lord.
And lordship means there is no room in the human heart with a sign saying:
“Jesus may not enter here.”
Maybe that is why this obscure passage feels heavier than expected.
The deepest question was never merely:
“Can Christians have sex during menstruation?”
The deeper question is:
When Scripture interrupts something I want, who gets the final word?
And that question exposes all of us.
Maybe your hidden issue has nothing to do with this particular subject.
Maybe yours is pornography.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe lust.
Maybe an emotional affair nobody knows about.
Maybe you have learned to rename compromise so you no longer have to call it sin.
Maybe you know exactly what God has been confronting, and you have spent months constructing theological loopholes around something your conscience already knows needs to be surrendered.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people managed to clean themselves up.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners could not save themselves, so Jesus came for them.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He bore sin at the cross.
He shed His blood for our redemption.
He rose from the grave.
And now forgiveness is offered not because our record is spotless, but because His sacrifice is sufficient.
That means conviction is not an invitation to hide.
It is an invitation to come home.
Peter had scandal.
The woman caught in adultery had scandal.
The Samaritan woman had scandal.
The thief beside Jesus had scandal.
The Corinthians had scandal.
We have scandal.
But scandal does not get the final sentence when Jesus enters the story.
Grace does.
Not cheap grace that baptizes whatever we want.
Transforming grace.
Grace that forgives and then teaches us to walk differently.
Grace that reaches into the places we are ashamed to discuss.
Grace that tells the truth without crushing the sinner.
Grace that says repentance is not the end of your story.
It can be the doorway into a new one.
That is why our theme will never simply be “behave better.”
Be honest.

And if Jesus has already rescued you from sexual sin, secret compromise, shame, addiction, or a broken past, consider sharing a piece of your testimony. Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance is possible and grace is real.
Let the conversation be gracious. Let it be biblical. Let it point people toward Christ.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves somebody loves Jesus.
It does not.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
God's grace is a gift.
But Christians can freely choose to support Gospel work and discipleship resources because they want biblical truth to keep reaching people.
And whether you ever purchase anything or not, we want Scripture in your hands.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who is drifting.
Invite the believer quietly struggling.
Invite the person who has stopped going to church.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the skeptic who thinks Christianity has nothing honest to say about real life.
Invite the person carrying a secret.
Because sometimes God begins rewriting a life when somebody finally has enough courage to open the page everyone else kept skipping.
And after all the Hebrew, all the difficult verses, all the theological questions, and all the uncomfortable discussion, remember what matters most:
Jesus is not afraid to enter the room you have been afraid to open.
